chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.text:
This article offers a critical analysis of Qur’anic verse 65:4 (Surah At-Talaq). This verse has often been cited in debates about the permissibility of child marriage in Islam. Traditional exegetical readings have interpreted the verse as legitimizing the divorce and remarriage of prepubescent girls (al-saghīrah), drawing on certain hadith reports that claim the Prophet’s marriage to Āʾishah at the age of six and consummated at nine. This study challenges such interpretations by conducting a close linguistic and contextual examination of the verse, alongside related Qur’anic passages such as 4:1–4, 4:6, 4:19, among others.

The analysis demonstrates that the language of verse 65:4 does not support its application to prepubescent girls, and that interpretations to this effect reflect cultural and political overlays rather than the Qur’an’s intended meaning. Instead, the Qur’an consistently frames marriage as a contractual union requiring maturity, consent, and accountability, thereby excluding the possibility of child marriage. Hadith reports that appear to endorse early marriage are considered only as part of the broader exegetical discourse but are shown to be secondary and methodologically less reliable when weighed against the Qur’an’s primary guidance.

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.text: The article concludes that Qur’an 65:4, properly understood, does not sanction child marriage. Rather, it reinforces the Qur’an’s overarching vision of marriage as a bond between responsible individuals, while early marriage practices should be understood as remnants of pre-Islamic cultural traditions not Qur’anic prescriptions.

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.text:
Non-Muslim polemicists frequently criticize Prophet Muhammad by alleging that he endorsed child marriage, citing hadith reports which claim that ʿĀʾishah was married at six and consummated at nine (3, 12, 13, 14, 15). These narratives are then invoked to portray both the Prophet and the Qur’an as condoning these practices. The traditionalist reliance on hadiths for historical context (4), however, overlooks their inconsistencies with the Qur’an’s authoritative guidance, which provides the definitive framework for Islamic jurisprudence (1, 19).

Classical exegetes such as al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Qurṭubī often accepted these reports as historically reliable, thereby normalizing the notion of prepubescent marriage. By contrast, modern scholarship has demonstrated how cultural, political, and patriarchal contexts shaped these interpretations, frequently obscuring the Qur’an’s ethical orientation (2, 7). In particular, scholars have shown how elevating contested hadith reports to near-canonical status distorted the Qur’an’s plain meaning and reflected sociocultural pressures more than divine intent (2, 5, 6). Unlike broader feminist frameworks that critique patriarchal structures in Islam more generally (8), this study builds on specific reinterpretations of the marriage verses to challenge hadith-based claims of child marriage and to highlight the Qur’an’s self-sufficient authority.

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.text:
The central question this article addresses is whether the Qur’an itself provides any textual or conceptual support for child marriage, or whether such claims arise solely from contested hadith reports and later exegetical traditions. This question carries particular significance today, as both polemicists and certain Muslim groups invoke these narrations in debates on Islam’s ethical stance regarding marriage, gender, and children’s rights.

To answer this, the article first examines the hadith literature, especially the narrations concerning ʿĀʾishah’s age, and then presents the Qur’an’s perspective, which demonstrates that marriage is intended exclusively for mature women (nisāʾ), not prepubescent girls (1). Through a holistic analysis of the Qur’an’s verse 65:4, g, and interrelated verses, followed by a reassessment of classical exegetical works—including those of al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, and Ibn Kathīr—this study argues that claims of Qur’anic sanction for child marriage are interpretive impositions rather than textual realities, and that the Qur’an’s framework is sufficient and authoritative in itself (1, 5, 10).

Let us now turn to the hadith literature that addresses the age of Aisha at the time of her marriage.

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.text:
Certain hadiths, cited by non-Muslim polemicists to criticize the Prophet and attack the divinity of the Qur'an, claim ʿĀʾishah was married at age six and the marriage consummated at nine, a narrative that stands in tension with the Qur'an's consistent emphasis on marriage involving adult women. These reports, found across canonical collections, include:

تَزَوَّجَ النبيُّ ﷺ عائِشَةَ وهي بنْتُ سِتِّ سِنِينَ، وبَنى بها وهي بنْتُ تِسْعٍ، ومَكَثَتْ عِنْدَهُ تِسْعًا

Sahīh al-Bukhārī — 5158: Narrated by ‘Urwah, it states: "The Prophet (ﷺ) wrote the (marriage contract) with ʿĀʾishah while she was six years old and consummated his marriage with her while she was nine years old and she remained with him for nine years (i.e., till his death)" (3).

Sahīh al-Bukhārī — 5133-5134: Narrated ʿĀʾishah: that the Prophet (ﷺ) married her when she was six years old and he consummated his marriage when she was nine years old, and then she remained with him for nine years (i.e., till his death) (3).

عَنْ عائِشَةَ، قالَتْ: تَزَوَّجَها رَسولُ اللهِ ﷺ وَهي بنْتُ سِتٍّ، وَبَنى بها وَهي بنْتُ تِسْعٍ، وَماتَ عَنْها وَهي بنْتُ ثَمانَ عَشْرَةَ

Sahīh Muslim — 1422: Narrated ʿĀʾishah: that the Prophet (ﷺ) married her when she was six years old and he consummated his marriage when she was nine years old, and then she remained with him for nine years (i.e., till his death) (12).

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.text:
- تزوَّجَني رسولُ اللهِ ﷺ وأنا بِنتُ سِتٍّ، ودخلَ عليَّ وأنا بِنتُ تِسعِ سنينَ، وكنتُ ألعَبُ بالبناتِ

Sunan an-Nasa’ī — 3378: It was narrated that 'Aishah said: "The Messenger of Allah married me when I was six, and consummated the marriage with me when I was nine, and I used to play with dolls (13).

تزوَّجَني رسولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ وأنا بنتُ ستِّ سنينَ فقدِمنا المدينةَ فنزلنا في بَني الحارثِ بنِ الخزرجِ فوعِكْتُ فتمرَّقَ شعري حتّى وفى لَه جُمَيْمةٌ فأتَتني أمِّي أمُّ رومانَ وإنِّي لفي أرجوحةٍ ومعي صواحباتٌ لي فصرخَت بي فأتيتُها وما أدري ما تريدُ فأخذَت بيدي فأوقَفَتني على بابِ الدّارِ وإنِّي لأنهجُ حتّى سَكَنَ بعضُ نفَسي ثمَّ أخذَتْ شيئًا من ماءٍ فمسَحت بهِ على وجهي ورأسي ثمَّ أدخلَتني الدّارَ فإذا نسوةٌ منَ الأنصارِ في بيتٍ فقُلنَ على الخيرِ والبرَكَةِ وعلى خيرِ طائرٍ فأسلَمَتني إليهنَّ فأصلَحنَ من شأني فلم يرُعني إلّا رسولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ ضُحًى فأسلَمَتني إليهِ وأنا يومئذٍ بنتُ تسعِ سنين

Sunan Ibn Mājah — 1877: Includes a detailed account of ʿĀʾishah’s age, illness, playing on an urjuhah (swing/seesaw) with friends, and the marriage consummation at nine (14).

هشام بن عروة عن أبيه قال قالت عائشة تزوجني رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وأنا ابنة ست سنين بمكة متوفى خديجة ودخل بي وأنا ابنة تسع سنين بالمدينة

Musnad Ahmad ibn Ḥanbal — 24139, 24602, 24603, 25636: Reiterate the claim of ʿĀʾishah’s marriage at six and consummation at nine (15).

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.text:
A related hadith in Sahih Muslim 1422c also mentions Āʾishah playing with dolls, stating: "I used to play with the dolls in the presence of the Prophet, and my girl friends also used to play with me." (12).

While these hadiths are classified as sahih (authentic), they rely heavily on narrators like Hisham ibn Urwah, whose reports from Iraq—where these narrations originate—have been questioned by classical scholars like Malik ibn Anas for potential memory issues or influence from local narrators (4, 11). Scholars note that such reports may reflect cultural practices or political motives from later periods, such as justifying early marriages for tribal alliances (7, 9), and modern critiques highlight how historical context influenced their authenticity (2).

While hadiths can offer historical context, their human-compiled nature makes them susceptible to errors, unlike the Qur'an’s divine precision (4, 5). The Quran’s textual and grammatical clarity, when examined across related verses, provides the authoritative guidance about marriage, reducing the need for reliance on such narrations (1, 5, 10).  It will be shown below that these hadiths present a narrative that contrasts with the Qur'an’s clear use of nisāʾ and its focus on maturity (e.g., 4:6, 4:19) (1).

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.text:
While the historical and methodological issues around the hadiths concerning Aisha’s age are substantive and warrant careful examination, ironically, verse 65:4 from Surah At-Talaq (The Divorce) is commonly cited by some traditional scholars, such as Ibn Kathir (discussed below) to support the notion of child marriage in the Qur’an. It is important to acknowledge that their interpretation is not independent of hadith influence. However, a close reading of the opening verse of this chapter explicitly establishes that the subject is a waiting period (iddah) for women in case of a divorce to establish paternity before potential remarriage. 65:1-4 expand upon the waiting period after divorce outlined in 2:228.

In particular, verse 65:4 provides further details about the waiting period for divorced women before remarriage (1):

وَاللَّائِي يَئِسْنَ مِنَ الْمَحِيضِ مِنْ نِسَائِكُمْ إِنِ ارْتَبْتُمْ فَعِدَّتُهُنَّ ثَلَاثَةُ أَشْهُرٍ وَاللَّائِي لَمْ يَحِضْنَ وَأُولَاتُ الْأَحْمَالِ أَجَلُهُنَّ أَنْ يَضَعْنَ حَمْلَهُنَّ وَمَنْ يَتَّقِ اللَّهَ يَجْعَلْ لَهُ مِنْ أَمْرِهِ يُسْرًا

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.text:
"And as for those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you have a doubt, their prescribed time shall be three months; and [the same applies to] those who have not yet menstruated. As for those who are pregnant, their prescribed time is until they deliver their burdens. And for everyone who is conscious of God, He makes it easy to obey His commandment." (65:4)

This verse reveals important insights through a lexical, morphological, syntactic, and grammatical agreement analysis. The key term is nisāʾ (نِسَاء), the plural of imraʾa (امرأة), meaning “women” in Arabic. Its triliteral root nūn sīn wāw occurs roughly 59 times in the Qur'an as only the noun nisā  (نِسَاء) and consistently refers to adult females in legal contexts such as marriage, divorce, and inheritance (e.g., 4:3, 4:11, 4:127).  The subject in the verse is nisāʾikum (“your women”), referring to adult female spouses. The feminine plural relative pronoun wallāʾī (وَاللَّائِي, “and those who”) refers back to nisāʾ in the preceding clause, and the third person plural verb yahidna (يَحِضْنَ, “have not menstruated”) agrees syntactically and morphologically with nisāʾ, maintaining adult women as the subject throughout the verse. Consequently, based on the linguistic and grammatical examination, there is no basis for interpreting the bolded portion of the verse as referring to prepubescent girls; it clearly addresses adult women.

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.text:
The phrase wallāʾī lam yahidna (“and those who have not yet menstruated”) can be understood as referring to two plausible categories of adult women who may not menstruate:

Women past menopause, who have naturally ceased menstruating due to age.

Women experiencing physiological conditions, such as amenorrhea caused by hormonal imbalances, stress, illness, or irregular cycles (1, 6).

Pregnant women are listed separately in the same verse, whose waiting period (iddah) concludes upon childbirth. Notably, the Quran does not use any of the Arabic terms like sabiyyah (young girl), jāriyah (maiden), or tiflah (child) when referring to marriageable females in this or any other context. The grammar and context of 65:4, when read alongside related verses, consistently employs nisāʾ (women), a term reserved for adult females. Claims that this verse permits child marriage have no textual or grammatical basis within the Qur’anic text. Yet, to understand how the controversial interpretations about the permissibility of child marriage took root, it is important to look at how classical exegetes interpreted this verse.

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.text:
Classical and post-classical exegetes offer insights into the scholarly traditions of their times. Their conclusions, however, stem from the principles that are tenuously linked to the Qur’anic text itself., Ibn Kathīr, for example, interpreted 65:4 to apply not only to post-menopausal women but also to girls who have not yet begun menstruating. In his Tafsīr al-Qur’ān al-ʿAzīm (vol. 10, p. 137), he  writes:

لِلصَّغِيرَةِ الَّتِي لَمْ تَحِضْ

(al-saghīrah allatī lam tahid — “the young girl who has not menstruated”) (16).

He explicitly includes prepubescent girls in the scope of the verse, aligning with many earlier commentators such as al-Tabarī and al-Qurtubī (17, 18). To support this view, Ibn Kathīr draws upon narrations, including the widely cited hadith reports about ʿĀʾishah’s marriage found in Sahīh al-Bukhārī and Sahīh Muslim. Moreover, in his tafsīr, a narration attributed to Ubayy bin Kaʿb is cited in the commentary on verse 65:4. According to this report, Ubayy asked the Prophet:

"O Allah's Messenger! When the Ayah in Surat Al-Baqarah was revealed prescribing the Iddah of divorce, some people in Al-Madinah said, 'There are still some women whose Iddah has not been mentioned in the Qur'an. There are the young, the old whose menstruation is discontinued, and the pregnant.' Later on, this Ayah was revealed (i.e 65:4)"

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.text:
This report appears in Ibn Abī Hātim’s tafsīr and is cited by later exegetes (16). However, like many tafsīr transmissions, it does not occur in the Sahīh hadith collections and is transmitted without a fully authenticated isnād. It is stated that the verse (65:4) was revealed to address categories with specific waiting periods. This tafsīr report suggests that Ubayy’s comment prompted clarification in the Qur’an that the prescribed ʿiddah applies to women who have not menstruated (i.e., young girls), those who have ceased menstruation (menopausal), and those who are pregnant. Ibn Kathīr synthesized verse 65:4 with the hadith reports about ʿĀʾishah and the tafsīr narration attributed to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, treating them collectively as evidence that the Qur’an encompasses prepubescent girls within its ruling on ʿiddah.

Ibn Kathīr built on earlier exegetes, notably al-Tabarī and al-Qurtubī, who form the backbone of the mainstream tafsīr tradition on 65:4. Al-Tabarī in his Jāmiʿ al-Bayān writes:

“As for those who have not menstruated, their waiting period is three months. So said the scholars regarding this matter. Ibn Zayd said: If a man divorces a young girl who has not menstruated, then her waiting period is three months.”

Al-Tabarī explicitly ties “those who have not menstruated” to al-saghīrah (the young girl) (17).

Al-Qurtubī in al-Jāmiʿ li-Ahkām al-Qur’ān likewise comments (18):

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.text:
“As for the waiting period of the one who has not menstruated due to her young age, her waiting period is three months.”

Ibn Kathīr largely reiterated these interpretations. Classical exegetes appear not to have considered alternative explanations for the phrase wa-llāʾī lam yahidna (“those who have not menstruated”), such as adult women who have not menstruated due to medical conditions (amenorrhea). Not only did they rely on received hadith and tafsīr reports, but they were also influenced by the prevailing social norms of their times. In his landmark book, Truth and Method (1989), Hans-Georg Gadamer argues that the interpreter’s prejudices and historicity must be taken into consideration, for all interpretation is shaped by preconceptions (21).

The disjuncture between the exegetical readings and the Qur’anic language on the issue demands a recalibration of our understanding of the norms of marriage in the Quran.

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.section: Exegetical Impositions at Odds with Qur’anic Linguistic Integrity
chunks.text: The dominant exegetical reading stands at odds with the Qur’an’s own linguistic and rhetorical patterns. The Qur’an never uses the term al-saghīrah (“the young girl”) when legislating marriage or divorce, but instead consistently employs the term nisāʾ (“women”). Moreover, if one accepts the claim that 65:4 was revealed in response to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb’s query about the demographic to which ʿiddah applies, it is striking that the verse does not open with the formula “They ask you…” (yasʾalūnaka / yastaftūnaka), as in other clarifying verses including those pertaining to women’s issues (2:222, 4:127, 4:176). Yet this is not the case: 65:4 begins with wa (“and”), a resumption particle indicating continuation from 64:1, which itself starts with yā ayyuhā al-nabiyu (“O Prophet”), showing that the divine guidelines on the waiting period after divorce were communicated directly to Muhammad without any prompting from his companions.

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.section: Exegetical Impositions at Odds with Qur’anic Linguistic Integrity
chunks.text: Furthermore, Kaʿb’s a priori classification—allegedly made prior to the revelation of 65:4—assumes young girls as a category which later exegetes then treated as authoritative. This reasoning exemplifies a form of circular logic or a ‘begging the question’ fallacy: the interpretation assumes the conclusion (that young girls are included) rather than allowing the Qur’an’s own text and grammar to define the verse’s scope. Such an interpretive imposition introduces human constructs into the reading of the divine speech, creating a tension between the Qur’an’s diction and the dominant exegetical tradition.

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.section: Exegetical Impositions at Odds with Qur’anic Linguistic Integrity
chunks.text: Ibn Kathīr’s commentary, produced in the 14th century under the Mamluk context, reflects reliance on inherited reports and cultural norms more than on independent linguistic analysis of the Qur’an. By treating hadith about ʿĀʾishah’s marriage and the tafsīr report of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb as decisive, he privileged tradition over a Qur’an-centered reading. His interpretation, in line with earlier exegetes, advanced views on child marriage that may owe more to prevailing historical culture than to the Qur’an’s own linguistic framework (16, 17, 18). Modern scholarship further illuminates how early Islamic marriage practices, influenced by pre-Islamic norms, shaped such exegesis (7), while political and sectarian agendas may have motivated hadith fabrication (9). Contemporary critiques have emphasized the need to re-evaluate these interpretations in light of the Qur'an's linguistic and textual integrity (2).

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.section: Marriage in the Qur’an: Adulthood, Consent, and Maturity
chunks.text:
The Qur'an 4:1 and 4:3-4, in Surah An-Nisa (The Women), further clarifies that marriage is for adult, mature women by using nisāʾ and emphasizing qualities tied to adulthood (1). The passage begins:

يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ اتَّقُوا رَبَّكُمُ الَّذِي خَلَقَكُمْ مِنْ نَفْسٍ وَاحِدَةٍ وَخَلَقَ مِنْهَا زَوْجَهَا وَبَثَّ مِنْهُمَا رِجَالًا كَثِيرًا وَنِسَاءً وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ الَّذِي تَسَاءَلُونَ بِهِ وَالْأَرْحَامَ إِنَّ اللَّهَ كَانَ عَلَيْكُمْ رَقِيبًا ()

O mankind! Be conscious of your Sustainer, who has created you out of one living entity, and out of it created its mate, and out of the two spread abroad a multitude of men and women. And remain conscious of God, in whose name you demand [your rights] from one another, and of these ties of kinship. Verily, God is ever watchful over you! (4:1)

Here, nisāʾ denotes adult women, counterparts to men (rijāl), in the context of creation and familial bonds. Verses 4:3–4 continue:

وَإِنْ خِفْتُمْ أَلَّا تُقْسِطُوا فِي الْيَتَامَى فَانْكِحُوا مَا طَابَ لَكُمْ مِنَ النِّسَاءِ مَثْنَى وَثُلَاثَ وَرُبَاعَ فَإِنْ خِفْتُمْ أَلَّا تَعْدِلُوا فَوَاحِدَةً أَوْ مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُكُمْ ذَلِكَ أَدْنَى أَلَّا تَعُولُوا () وَآتُوا النِّسَاءَ صَدُقَاتِهِنَّ نِحْلَةً فَإِنْ طِبْنَ لَكُمْ عَنْ شَيْءٍ مِنْهُ نَفْسًا فَكُلُوهُ هَنِيئًا مَرِيئًا()

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.section: Marriage in the Qur’an: Adulthood, Consent, and Maturity
chunks.text:
"And if you have reason to fear that you might not act equitably towards orphans, then marry from among women such as are lawful to you – [even] two, or three, or four: but if you have reason to fear that you might not be able to treat them with equal fairness, then [only] one – or [from among] those whom you rightfully possess. This will make it more likely that you will not deviate from the right course. And give unto women their marriage portions in the spirit of a gift; but if they, of their own accord, give up unto you aught thereof, then enjoy it with pleasure and good cheer." (4:3–4)

These verses use nisāʾ to describe marriageable women, emphasizing justice, consent, and financial responsibilities like dowers, which point to adult partners capable of mutual agreement and marital duties. The reference to orphans in 4:3 is linked to 4:6 which states:

وَابْتَلُوا الْيَتَامَى حَتَّى إِذَا بَلَغُوا النِّكَاحَ فَإِنْ آنَسْتُمْ مِنْهُمْ رُشْدًا فَادْفَعُوا إِلَيْهِمْ أَمْوَالَهُمْ وَلَا تَأْكُلُوهَا إِسْرَافًا وَبِدَارًا أَنْ يَكْبَرُوا وَمَنْ كَانَ غَنِيًّا فَلْيَسْتَعْفِفْ وَمَنْ كَانَ فَقِيرًا فَلْيَأْكُلْ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ فَإِذَا دَفَعْتُمْ إِلَيْهِمْ أَمْوَالَهُمْ فَأَشْهِدُوا عَلَيْهِمْ وَكَفَى بِاللَّهِ حَسِيبًا ()

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.section: Marriage in the Qur’an: Adulthood, Consent, and Maturity
chunks.text:
And test the orphans [in your charge] until they reach the age of marriage; then, if you find them to be mature of mind, hand over to them their possessions; and do not consume them extravagantly or hastily in anticipation of their growing up. And let him who is rich abstain entirely [from his ward’s property]; and let him who is poor partake thereof in a fair manner. And when you hand over to them their possessions, let there be witnesses on their behalf – although God is sufficient as a witness. (4:6)

The Qur'an requires waiting for orphans to reach "the age of marriage" (balaghū an-nikāh) before entrusting property and mental maturity (rushd), underscoring the principle that legal and social responsibility requires adulthood. Read holistically, 4:1–4 with 4:6 indicates that marriage is intended for adult women who have reached mental maturity, consistent with the Quran’s text and grammar.

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.section: Marriage in the Qur’an: Adulthood, Consent, and Maturity
chunks.text: The Quran’s marriage rulings consistently use nisāʾ to refer to marriageable females, as seen in verses like 2:221-223, 4:22–24, and 4:25, which address believing women capable of consent and responsibility. Verses 4:19 and 4:21 present marriage as a solemn covenant (mīthāqan ghalīzan) and emphasize mutual consent and kindness in marriage, indicating partners with the capacity for informed decision-making (6, 8). The Qur'an’s silence on prepubescent marriage, combined with its emphasis on reaching the age of maturity (e.g., 4:6), confirms that marriage is between adult males and females. The discussion in 2:222 assumes women in marital relations are menstruating, and of reproductive age. In 65:4, "those who have not menstruated" is more plausibly understood as referring to adult women with physiological conditions, not children, as no Qur'anic term or context supports such an interpretation. Qur’an 24:58-59 establishes that children are subject to special privacy rules until they reach puberty (hulm)—an age of discernment and maturity—after which they are treated as adults responsible for observing household boundaries similar to those senior to them. Taken together, these verses reveal a consistent framework: marriage in the scripture is firmly grounded in adulthood, responsibility, and consent (1, 2, 5, 6, 8).

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.section: Marriage in the Qur’an: Adulthood, Consent, and Maturity
chunks.text: Some hadiths mention puberty or consent in marriage, partially aligning with the Qur'an’s emphasis on maturity. However, those hadiths claiming ʿĀʾishah was a child bride and played with dolls or on a swing with friends conflict with the Quran’s consistent use of nisāʾ and its focus on adult females (e.g., 4:6, 4:19). As human-compiled texts, hadiths are inherently fallible, whereas the Quran represents God’s perfect, infallible word. Verses such as 2:221–223, 4:1-4, 4:6, 4:19, and 4:21 collectively emphasize that marriage is intended for older menstruating females capable of consent and responsibility, providing a clear and complete framework (1, 10). By relying solely on the Qur'an’s text, grammar, and interconnected verses, one can discern God’s guidance on marriage, without needing to depend on hadiths that introduce distortions or culturally influenced interpretations (5, 10, 11). This raises a broader methodological question, how should themes such as marriage guide our interpretation?

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.section: Text, Grammar, and Context: A Qur’an-Only Method of Interpretation
chunks.text: The Qur'an, as God’s infallible word, claims that it is the sole and sufficient authority for divine guidance. It is a clarification and detailed explanation of everything (16:89, 6:114-115, 7:52, 12:111, 17:9). To understand its message accurately including the complete criteria on marriage, one must study the text, grammar, and related verses as a whole, ensuring interpretations remain faithful to its divine intent. Hadiths claiming that ʿĀʾishah was married at six and consummated at nine introduce a narrative of child marriage entirely absent from the Qur'an’s framework, which emphasizes adult women (nisāʾ) and maturity (e.g., 4:6, 4:19, 4:21). The Qur'an consistently treats women as legally competent adults—able to own property, take oaths, bear witness, and bear full accountability—roles that prepubescent girls cannot fulfill. These hadith reports and the later exegetical sources, shaped by post-prophetic cultural and political contexts, rely on narrators whose reliability has been debated (4, 6, 10, 11). Such hadith reports, often shaped by early Islamic marriage practices that included pre-Islamic customs (7), may reflect political or sectarian motivations for fabrication (9). Modern critiques further highlight their inconsistencies with the Qur’an’s ethical framework (2).

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.section: Text, Grammar, and Context: A Qur’an-Only Method of Interpretation
chunks.text: The Qur'an’s holistic guidance—seen in verses like 2:221–223, 4:1–4, 4:6, 4:19, and 65:4—frames marriage as a covenant between mature females and males, emphasizing consent, responsibility, and readiness (1, 8). Muhammad, the final messenger through whom the Qur'an was revealed, is understood to have been a good example for the believers (33:21) suggesting his actions aligned with divine principles, and the reports suggesting he married a prepubescent ʿĀʾishah are best read as later attributions which stand at odds with Qur'an's own linguistic and rhetorical patterns. Such inconsistencies underscore the importance of critically reevaluating hadith literature that conflicts with the divine guidance.

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.section: Text, Grammar, and Context: A Qur’an-Only Method of Interpretation
chunks.text: Typically, hadith are understood as the sayings of the Prophet meant to “explain” the divine scripture. Yet in this case, narrators introduce an entirely new demographic— prepubescent girls—into the marriage context potentially assuming the conclusion a priori through circular reasoning or 'begging the question' fallacy without any linguistic basis in the Quran. In mainstream Islam, narrators of the major hadith collections are generally regarded as reliable and beyond reproach, even when the reports attributed to them do not stand up to scrutiny when they are critically evaluated and benchmarked against the Quran. Questioning such reports can provoke reprisal from devout followers who treat them as final authority, discouraging intellectual discourse. The Quran, however, grants no such immunity to human transmitters. It explicitly warns that even some of the Prophet’s contemporaries were hypocrites whose words and actions were unreliable (63:1–3, 9:107, 33:12–13), underscoring the need to evaluate all reports carefully and independently (49:6), and reaching one's conclusions on the basis of critical examination and logical inference (39:18) with the word of God as the ultimate standard of truth.

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.section: Text, Grammar, and Context: A Qur’an-Only Method of Interpretation
chunks.text:
The Qur’an precisely encodes divine guidance in its text, grammar, and interwoven verses, which can be decoded by examining it from within—without reliance on external sources—thereby preventing false assumptions, erroneous interpretations, and intellectual tampering.

It must be engaged directly to ensure that the true meaning of the text is not distorted by political and cultural impositions.

A close study of the Qur’an’s text and grammar makes it clear that it elevates women's status by requiring adulthood and consent and does not reintroduce the hadith-based narrative of supporting pre-Islamic cultural practices of prepubescent marriage.

The Qur’an consistently uses the term nisāʾ (women) in marriage rulings (2:221–223, 4:22–25), and emphasizes mutual consent (4:19), solemn covenant (mīthāq ghalīz, 4:21), and maturity (4:6), all of which presuppose adult partners with the capacity for responsibility.

Verse 2:222 addresses menstruation in the context of marital relations, indicating that the Qur’an links marriage and sexual relations to women who have reached biological maturity.

Even in 65:4—often misinterpreted—the phrase “those who have not menstruated” is better understood as referring to post-menopausal women or women with medical conditions such as amenorrhea, not children, since the Qur’an provides no language permitting child marriage.

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.section: Text, Grammar, and Context: A Qur’an-Only Method of Interpretation
chunks.text:
Many modern Muslim-majority countries, recognizing the Qur’an’s emphasis on maturity and responsibility, have set minimum age laws (e.g., 16 or 18), aligning with its principles of justice and protection (20).

Through careful intellectual analysis, Muslims can recover God’s guidance not only on marriage but also on other societal issues, grounded solely on the Qur’an’s clear and infallible revelation (16:89, 6:114–115, 7:52).

This Qur’an only method guards against external intrusions and socio-cultural assumptions, which, as is evident in the case of traditional exegetes, have shaped, and in the case of the age of marriage, distorted interpretation.

chunks.title: The Qur'an, Hadith, and the Debate on Marriageable Age: A Textual Analysis
chunks.text: This study has critically examined the Qur’an, Hadith, and exegetical traditions in relation to the debate on child marriage, with particular attention to Qur’an 65:4 and hadith reports concerning the age of ʿĀʾishah. The analysis demonstrates that the Qur’an consistently frames marriage as a contractual union requiring maturity, consent, and responsibility, offering no textual support for child marriage. Reports suggesting otherwise reflect cultural and historical contexts rather than the Qur’an’s ethical directives. By prioritizing Qur’anic guidance, this article calls for a re-reading of the tradition that upholds human dignity, protects children, and aligns with Islam’s higher objectives of justice and mercy. The study underscores the necessity of revisiting classical interpretations on the basis of comprehensive Qur'anic analysis, which in this case converges with contemporary understandings of children’s rights and welfare. Ultimately, it emphasizes that Islam envisions marriage as a responsible partnership rooted in moral accountability, not a cultural practice devoid of ethical grounding.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān

Azfar Samin

azfar.samin@gmail.com

Abstract

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text: This article reexamines two long-standing assumptions in Islamic tradition: that Prophet Muḥammad was illiterate and that the Qurʾān was first codified only under the caliph ʿUthmān. Through a pan-textual and morphological analysis (RYDING 2005; OWENS 2013; HOLES 2018), it argues that the Qurʾānic term ʾummī denotes “unscriptured”—one without prior revelation—rather than “unlettered” (Q 2:78). Internal linguistic evidence, including the reflexive verb iktatabahā (Q 25:5) contrasted with causative forms, together with references to an inscribed kitāb (Q 52:2–3), ṣuḥuf and safarah (Q 98:2; Q 80:13–15) and qalam (Q 68:1; 96:4), strongly suggests that writing was integral to revelation from its inception and that the Prophet personally engaged in writing the scripture (Q 25:5; 29:48). Muhammad is the central referent in both Q 25:5 and Q 29:48, and the temporal qualifier qablihi (“before it”) in Q 29:48 confines the statement to the Prophet’s prior non-exposure to earlier Abrahamic texts. These findings align with philological and codicological research (NEUWIRTH 2019; PUIN 1996; SADEGHI and GOUDARZI 2012; FEDELI 2018) demonstrating the existence of written Qurʾānic material during or immediately after the Prophet’s lifetime. The study also traces how later exegetes—AL-ṬABARĪ, AL-QURṬUBĪ, and IBN KATHĪR—recast ʾummī as “illiterate” through reinterpretations and reinforce the ḥadīth view of prophetic illiteracy as miraculous proof. Engaging with the text directly, the article recenters the Qurʾān’s self-description as al-Kitāb—a text both recited and written—affirming that revelation presupposed literacy, inscription, and textual preservation from the outset.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text: Keywords: Arabic morphology; early Qurʾānic codification; prophetic literacy; Qurʾānic philology; textual transmission; ummī; written revelation

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
It is widely believed in mainstream Islam that Prophet Muḥammad was an ummī—an illiterate individual who could neither read nor write. This understanding, however, rests not on Qurʾānic language but on much later exegetical and ḥadīth traditions. Within the Qurʾān itself, the adjective ʾummī (أُمِّيّ) never denotes “unable to read or write.” Linguistically, it describes one who has not been exposed to any previous revelation—a person belonging to a community other than the People of the Book (Jews and Christians).

This article begins by reconstructing that original Qurʾānic meaning through linguistic and textual analysis. It first clarifies how the Qurʾān defines ʾummī and its plural ʾummiyyūn, then turns to internal linguistic evidence—particularly verses Q 25:5; Q 52:2–3; Q 80:13–15; and Q 98:2—which depict the Prophet as directly engaged with written revelation. It subsequently argues, through a pan-textual analysis, that the Qurʾān presents itself as a written text (al-Kitāb) from its very inception—contrary to later extra-Qurʾānic claims that compilation occurred only under the caliphate of ʿUthmān.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text: Methodologically, this study treats the Qurʾān as a self-referential discourse whose morphology, semantics, and internal cross-references together provide the primary framework for clarifying its key terms and narrative logic—without recourse to external exegetical or historical systems. This linguistic approach does not dismiss the post-Qurʾānic tradition; rather, it adopts a Qurʾān-centric method that first defines its vocabulary (ʾummī, kitāb, ṣuḥuf, qalam) through internal coherence before engaging later commentary. Section 5 elaborates on this framework, situating it within a broader hermeneutical tradition that views linguistic analysis as an act of faithful inquiry rather than polemical revisionism. This pan-textual approach reflects the Qurʾān’s own invitation to examine its internal coherence and consistency (Q 4:82), treating semantic harmony across verses as an interpretive principle rather than subordinating Qurʾānic language to later theological assumptions.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text: Finally, the paper situates its findings within contemporary philological and codicological scholarship—most notably the works of NEUWIRTH, PUIN, SADEGHI, and FEDELI—which have questioned the conventional chronology of the Qurʾān’s written codification. While fully acknowledging the deep reverence Muslims hold for the Qurʾān and its Messenger, this article seeks to recover—from the Qurʾān itself, as God’s infallible word and “a clarification and detailed explanation of everything” (Q 16:89; cf. Q 6:114–115; Q 7:52; Q 12:111; Q 17:9)—its own linguistic testimony, thereby clarifying how certain theological interpretations evolved over time.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
وَمِنْهُمْ أُمِّيُّونَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ الْكِتَابَ إِلَّا أَمَانِيَّ وَإِنْ هُمْ إِلَّا يَظُنُّونَ

Wa-min-hum ʾummiyyūn lā yaʿlamūna al-kitāba illā ʾamāniyya wa-in hum illā yaẓunnūn.

“And among them are unlettered ones who do not know the Scripture except in wishful thinking, but they are only assuming.” (Q 2:78)

Here the self-referential Qurʾān itself defines ʾummiyyūn as “those who do not know the Book.” Their deficiency lies in ignorance of revelation, not in the inability to read or write. They replace revealed knowledge with ʾamānī (“wishful thinking”) and ẓann (“assumptions”).

The word ʾUmmī (أُمِّيّ) is commonly connected to the root hamza mīm mīm (أ م م)— “source, mother, community”—following the fuʿʿī pattern, which denotes belonging. Thus, ʾummī literally means “one from among the people,” or “one of the common, unscriptured folk.”

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.section: Other Qurʾānic Uses of Ummī and Ummiyyūn
chunks.text:
The word ummi occurs in the Qur’an six times, four times as a noun (Q 2:78; Q 3:20, Q 3:75; Q 62:2) and twice as an adjective (Q 7:157-158). Let's look at the remaining five occurrences below:

Verse | Phrase / Context | Description and Semantic Function

Q 3:20 | “…wa-qul lilladhīna ūtū al-kitāba wa-al-ʾummiyyīn…” | Contrasts those given the Book (Ahl al-Kitāb) with al-ʾummiyyīn—the unscriptured peoples lacking prior revelation.

Q 3:75 | “…dhālika bi-annahum qālū laysa ʿalaynā fī al-ʾummiyyīna sabīl…” | Explicit mention of al-ʾummiyyīn (“those without prior scripture”); contrasts Ahl al-Kitāb’s in-group ethics toward the ʾummiyyūn, reinforcing that ʾummiyyūn ≠ illiterate, but “non-scriptured others.”

Q 7:157–158 | “…al-nabiyy al-ʾummī…” “…wa-rasūlihi al-nabiyyi al-ʾummiyy…” | Refers to “the Prophet from among the unscriptured”—one raised without earlier scripture who becomes its first bearer.

Q 62:2 | “Huwa alladhī baʿatha fī al-ʾummiyyīn rasūlan minhum…” | Describes a Messenger raised among the unscriptured nation, tasked with reciting, purifying, and teaching the Book.

Hence the word ʾummiyyīn is contrasted with the people of the book in the Qur’an. Ahl al-Kitāb = people who possess earlier scripture. ʾUmmiyyūn = people who do not.

Thus, when the Qurʾān calls Muhammad al-nabiyy al-ʾummī (Q 7:157), it simply means: “The Prophet from a people without previous revelation.” Before revelation, he shared their ʾummiyyah; afterwards, he became teacher of the Book (Q 62:2).

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
Another verse that supports the viewpoint that Muhammad was never exposed to any prior scripture is Q 29:48

وَمَا كُنتَ تَتْلُوا۟ مِن قَبْلِهِۦ مِن كِتَـٰبٍ وَلَا تَخُطُّهُۥ بِيَمِينِكَ إِذًا لَّٱرْتَابَ ٱلْمُبْطِلُونَ

Wa-mā kunta tatlū min qablihi min kitābin wa-lā takhuṭṭuhu bi-yamīnika idhan la-irtāba al-mubṭilūn.

“And you did not recite before it any scripture, nor did you write it with your right hand, otherwise the falsifiers would have doubted.” (Q 29:48)

Muhammad is being accused of deriving the Qurʾān from earlier Abrahamic texts. The use of qablihi (“before it”) is key, for it temporally binds the argument by indicating not illiteracy but prior non-exposure. The Qurʾān rejects the accusation with this verse, stating that he did not engage with earlier scripture either orally or in written form before this revelation, rather than asserting permanent illiteracy.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.section: From Ummī to Bearer of the Book
chunks.text:
هُوَ الَّذِي بَعَثَ فِي الْأُمِّيِّينَ رَسُولًا مِّنْهُمْ يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتِهِ وَيُزَكِّيهِمْ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ الْكِتَابَ وَالْحِكْمَةَ

Huwa alladhī baʿatha fī al-ummiyyīna rasūlan minhum yatlū ʿalayhim āyātihi wa-yuzakkīhim wa-yuʿallimuhumu al-kitāba wa-al-ḥikmata wa-in kānū min qablu la-fī ḍalālin mubīn.

“It is He who has sent among the unlettered a Messenger from themselves reciting to them His verses and purifying them and teaching them the Book and wisdom - although they were before in clear error.” (Q 62:2)

Logical reasoning would dictate that a messenger who teaches the Book must engage with it textually—since ‘teaching the Book’ (yuʿallimuhum al-kitāb) semantically presupposes familiarity with both its content and medium. The Qurʾān therefore presents Muhammad as transformed from unexposed to revelation into its first reader and teacher.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.section: Literacy in the Qurʾān: Internal Evidence
chunks.text:
The following section examines the Qurʾān itself for evidence that the Prophet Muhammad could both read and write, and that the Qurʾān was being written down from the very beginning of revelation—not merely memorized orally and committed to writing decades later. This internal linguistic evidence challenges the extra-Qurʾānic narrative found in later historical and ḥadīth sources, which claim that the Qurʾān existed only in memory during the Prophet’s lifetime and was written down formally under the caliph ʿUthmān.

In contrast, the Qurʾānic text repeatedly depicts itself as a “kitāb” (written book) right from the very beginning (Q 2:2), described as inscribed, recorded, and transmitted through pages and scribes, indicating that the act of writing was integral to revelation from its earliest moment.

We now turn to the first of these passages—Q 25:5—which linguistically affirms that the Prophet himself was accused of writing the material, not merely reciting it.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
In Surah al furqān verses 4 and 5, we note the unbelievers are making the accusation of the Qur'an being an invention originating from historical stories as opposed to revelation from God. Clearly the interlocutor being addressed here is Prophet Muhammad. The entrenched belief that Muhammad was ummī—interpreted as “unable to read or write”—has directly influenced how translators render Qurʾān Q 25:5.

وَقَالُوا أَسَاطِيرُ الْأَوَّلِينَ اِكْتَتَبَهَا فَهِيَ تُمْلَىٰ عَلَيْهِ بُكْرَةً وَأَصِيلًا

Wa-qālū ʾasāṭīru al-awwalīn iktatabahā fa-hiya tumlā ʿalayhi bukratan wa-ʾaṣīlā.

“And they say, "Legends of the former peoples which he has written down, and they are dictated to him morning and afternoon” (Q 25:5)

Here, due to theological orthodoxy, many translators render iktatabahā as “caused to be written,” implying that the Prophet dictated revelation to others. For example, YUSUF ALI (1934) translates Q 25:5 as follows:

“And they say: ‘Tales of the ancients, which he has caused to be written: and they are dictated before him morning and evening.’” (Q 25:5)

The key verb اِكْتَتَبَهَا (iktatabahā) is a Form VIII (اِفْتَعَلَ) verb derived from the root ك ت ب (k-t-b) “to write.”

Form VIII verbs insert a t-infix after the first radical, marking self-directed or reflexive action.

Hence iktatabahā means:

“He wrote them down (for himself).”

If the Qurʾān—whose language is exact to the letter—had intended “he caused them to be written”, it would have used one of the causative patterns instead:

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
Form II (kat-taba كَتَّبَ) → “to make someone write.” Form IV (ʾaktaba أَكْتَبَ) → “to caused to be written / to dictate.”

Because the verse employs Form VIII, not Form II or IV, the causative reading is grammatically untenable. The morphology itself restricts the meaning to a reflexive act—“he wrote,” not “he had written.”

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.section: Reflexive vs Causative in Arabic Grammar
chunks.text:
Before turning to the control example in Q 25:4, it helps to clarify these grammatical categories.

Reflexive → The subject performs the action upon or for itself.

Examples:

ittakhadha (Q 4:125) = “to take for oneself, to adopt.”

iktatabahā (Q 25:5) = “he wrote them down.”

Causative → The subject causes another agent to perform the action.

Examples:

arsala (Q 13:38) = “to cause to go/to send forth.”

aʿlama (Q 2:33) = “to cause someone to know.”

This distinction is foundational in Arabic morphology:

the presence of the prefix ʾa- (Form IV) signals externalization of the act, while the t-infix of Form VIII signals internalization—action reflected back on the subject. Hence, if the meaning was intended to be “he caused to be written down” the Form IV verb would have been aktaba which is not the case in Q 25:5.

Arabic reference grammars consistently note that Form VIII (iftaʿala) verbs typically convey reflexive or middle meanings—actions directed toward or performed for oneself—whereas Form IV (ʾafʿala) verbs are causative, indicating that the subject causes another to perform the act (e.g., ʾaktaba “he caused to write” vs. iktataba “he wrote for himself”; cf. RYDING 2005; OWENS 2013; HOLES 2018).

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
وَقَالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا إِنْ هَٰذَا إِلَّا إِفْكٌ اِفْتَرَاهُ وَأَعَانَهُ عَلَيْهِ قَوْمٌ آخَرُونَ

Wa-qāla alladhīna kafarū in hādhā illā ʾifkun iftarāhu wa-aʿānahu ʿalayhi qawmun ʾākharūn.

“And those who disbelieve say, "This [Qur'an] is not except a falsehood he invented, and another people assisted him in it." But they have committed an injustice and a lie.” (Q 25:4)

Here, the Qurʾān itself prepares the reader for Q 25:5 by juxtaposing two distinct verb patterns—Form VIII and Form IV—in a single verse. This morphological contrast provides an internal linguistic clue.

Verb (Arabic / Transliteration) | Form & Root | Literal Meaning | Agency Type / Function

اِفْتَرَاهُ (iftarāhu) | Form VIII — ف ر ي (f-r-y) | “He fabricated it himself.” | Reflexive / self-initiated action; the act originates within the subject.

أَعَانَهُ (aʿānahu) | Form IV — ع و ن (ʿ-w-n) | “He caused others to help / they helped him.” | Causative / transitive action; the subject causes another agent to perform the act.

In one verse, the Qurʾān employs both forms side by side to distinguish two kinds of agency:

self-initiated (Form VIII), and

externally caused (Form IV).

This internal contrast showcases the Qurʾān’s morphological precision—when God intends a causative meaning, He employs Form IV (or Form II); when He intends a self-directed action, He employs Form VIII.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.section: Form VIII Verbs in the Qurʾān: Morphological Boundaries of Agency
chunks.text:
A survey of Qurʾānic Form VIII verbs demonstrates a consistent semantic pattern: all denote self-directed or reciprocal agency. The following table summarizes representative examples.

Root | Form VIII Verb | Verse(s) | Sense in context | Reflexive / Reciprocal / Causative?

ف-ر-ي | اِفْتَرَى (iftarā) | Q 25:4, 10:38 | fabricate for oneself | Reflexive/self-initiated

أ-خ-ذ |  |  | Take/adopt for oneself | Reflexive/self-directed

أ-خ-ذ | اِتَّخَذَ (ittakhadha) | Q 2:51, etc. | take/adopt for oneself | Reflexive

س-ل-م | اِسْتَسْلَمَ (istaslama) | Q 4:125 | submit oneself | Reflexive

ش-ر-ى | اِشْتَرَى (ishtarā) | Q 2:16, etc. | purchase for oneself | Reflexive (“to acquire”)

ب-ي-ع | اِبْتَغَى (ibtaghā) | Q 4:114, etc. | seek for oneself | Reflexive

ذ-ك-ر | اِذْتَكَرَ (idhthakara) | Q 54:17 | remember for oneself | Reflexive

ط-ه-ر | اِطَّهَرَ (ittahara) | Q 9:108 | purify oneself | Reflexive

و-ق-ى | اِتَّقَى (ittaqā) → مُتَّقِينَ (muttaqīn) (derived participle) | Q 2:2 etc. | Act with conscious self-restraint | Reflexive – semantic derivative (active participle from Form VIII)

This pattern is not incidental but structural. The Qurʾān’s internal verb system distinguishes sharply between Forms IV, II (causative) and VIII (reflexive). That consistency lends decisive grammatical weight to the reflexive reading of (Q 25:5).

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.section: Form VIII Verbs in the Qurʾān: Morphological Boundaries of Agency
chunks.text:
This consistent internal morphology confirms that iktatabah—“he wrote them down for himself”—rather than any causative procurement (“he had them written”). The Qurʾān’s own morphology eliminates ambiguity: the Prophet’s opponents accused him of writing, not of employing scribes.

Within the Qurʾān itself, Form VIII (iftaʿala) verbs uniformly express self-directed or reciprocal action; none function causatively. The contrast between iftarāhu (Form VIII, Q 25:4) and aʿānahu (Form IV, same verse) confirms this morphological boundary. Accordingly, iktatabahā (Q 25:5) must mean “he wrote them down for himself,” not “he caused them to be written.” Post-Qurʾānic lexicons expanded the sense to include causative procurement, likely under exegetical pressure to align with the later doctrine of prophetic illiteracy. The Qurʾān’s own linguistic system, however, admits only the reflexive sense.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
The widespread rendering of iktatabahā as “he had them written down” in many modern translations does not arise from grammar but from post-Qurʾānic theological presuppositions reinforced by later ḥadīth narratives and exegetical aims.

Among the most frequently cited reports is the account of the first revelation in ṢAḤĪḤ AL-BUKHĀRĪ (4953), where the Angel Jibrīl commands the Prophet, “Read!” (Iqraʾ), and he replies:

“I do not know how to read.” — (ṢAḤĪḤ AL-BUKHĀRĪ, Kitāb Badʾ al-Waḥy, ḥadīth 4953)

This narration has long been interpreted as evidence that the Prophet was unable to read or write. Yet linguistically, the phrase mā ana bi-qāriʾin (“I am not a reader”) does not necessarily mean “I cannot read,” but rather “I have not read [any text or scripture].” The statement therefore reflects the Prophet’s lack of prior engagement with written revelation, not an inherent inability to read.

Another well-known report appears in ṢAḤĪḤ AL-BUKHĀRĪ (1913):

“We are an unlettered nation; we neither write, nor know accounts.” — (ṢAḤĪḤ AL-BUKHĀRĪ, Kitāb al-Ṣawm, ḥadīth 1913)

This hadith describes the cultural condition of the early Arabs (ummiyyūn)—a society without a written tradition of scripture—rather than asserting that the Prophet personally lacked literacy.

Nevertheless, later exegetes extrapolated this collective description to the Prophet himself, interpreting ummī as “illiterate.”

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.section: Exegetical Reframing: Illiteracy as Proof of the Miracle
chunks.text:
Early commentators—especially AL-ṬABARĪ (d. 310 AH), followed by AL-QURṬUBĪ (d. 671 AH) and IBN KATHĪR (d. 774 AH)—adopted this understanding of ʾummī to advance a theological argument: that the Qurʾān’s eloquence and literary perfection were miraculous precisely because it was revealed to an “unlettered” man.

In AL-ṬABARĪ’s Tafsīr (on Q 7:157), the Prophet is described as “كان أميًّا لا يكتب” (“he was ummī, he did not write”). AL-QURṬUBĪ follows this, stating that Muḥammad’s illiteracy was part of God’s wisdom, “lest the disbelievers say he learned it from previous scriptures.” IBN KATHĪR reiterates this reading, citing Ibn ʿAbbās: “The ummiyyūn are those who do not write” (on Q 2:78).

This line of reasoning served a theological and apologetic purpose: If the Prophet could not read or write, then the Qurʾān’s literary power must be divine in origin, not human composition.

Thus, the doctrine of prophetic illiteracy became an article of orthodoxy, transforming the word ʾummī from “one without prior scripture” into “one who cannot read or write.”

Furthermore, Q 29:48 became central to this exegetical framework:

وَمَا كُنتَ تَتْلُوا۟ مِن قَبْلِهِۦ مِن كِتَـٰبٍ وَلَا تَخُطُّهُۥ بِيَمِينِكَ

“And you did not recite before it any scripture, nor did you write it with your right hand…” (Q 29:48)

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.section: Exegetical Reframing: Illiteracy as Proof of the Miracle
chunks.text:
However, as discussed earlier, the temporal qualifier qablihi (“before it”) confines the statement to the Prophet’s prior non-exposure to earlier Abrahamic texts revealed to Jewish and Christian communities who disputed with him and potentially accused him of deriving the Qurʾān from their scriptures (Q 29:46). IBN KATHĪR, like other exegetes, in his commentary on Q 29:48 narrows the definition of ummī to a prophet “unable to write even one line or one letter” and that “This is how the Messenger of Allah will remain until the Day of Resurrection” without taking into account the time bound nature of the initial clause in Q 29:48.

When read carefully, the verse also implies Muhammad could write with his right hand (bi-yamīnika), a further indication that writing with one’s own hand is a conceivable category for Muhammad; otherwise the clause becomes rhetorically strange.

The verse Q 29:48 coheres naturally with the Qurʾānic usage of ummī and addresses lack of prior scriptural exposure rather than an enduring inability to read or write.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
Once this belief took root, it shaped how Q 25:5 was read and translated. Since exegetes assumed that the Prophet could not write, they reinterpreted iktatabahā—a Form VIII (reflexive) verb meaning “he wrote [it] down for himself”—as if it were Form IV (causative), “he caused it to be written.”

This theological constraint overrode grammar: the morphology of the verb clearly indicates self-action, yet translators rendered it as causative to align with inherited doctrine. As a result, linguistic precision gave way to theological consistency.

A pan-textual linguistic reading of the Qurʾān, however, restores the original sense: the Prophet’s opponents accused him of personally writing down revelation that was being dictated (tumlā) to him, which they dismissed as “tales of the ancients.” The term tumlā reinforces the image of a message both heard and inscribed, directly by its recipient.

In summary, the belief that Muhammad could not read or write originates not from the Qurʾān’s language but from post-Qurʾānic exegesis and ḥadīth interpretation. Exegetes sought to elevate the Prophet’s illiteracy into a miraculous proof of divine revelation, unintentionally distorting how verses like Q 25:5 were read and translated. Grammar, however, preserves the original meaning: iktatabahā— “he wrote them down for himself.”

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text: Having established from morphology that the Prophet personally engaged in writing, we now examine the Qurʾān’s broader self-presentation as a written revelation. Further textual evidence within the Qurʾān is provided showing that the revelation was being written down from the very beginning, not compiled posthumously after the Prophet’s lifetime.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
رَسُولٌۭ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ يَتْلُوا۟ صُحُفًۭا مُّطَهَّرَةًۭ

Rasūlun mina llāhi yatlū ṣuḥufan muṭahharah.

“A messenger from God, reciting purified scriptures.” (Q 98:2)

The triliteral root ṣ-ḥ-f (ص-ح-ف) connotes to spread open, inscribe, display in writing. Ṣuḥuf (plural of ṣaḥīfah) literally means “pages” or “scrolls.”

When the plural ṣuḥuf appears, its Qurʾānic usage overwhelmingly refers to inscribed, textual forms of revelation — not oral, metaphorical, or eschatological concepts — with only rare exceptions. The following table shows that except for Q 81:10 (eschatological “records of deeds”) and Q 43:71 (platters of gold), every occurrence of ṣuḥuf in the Qurʾān unambiguously denotes written, textual material.

Verse | Phrase | Immediate Context | Semantic Function

Q 20:133 | “Aw lam ta’tihim bayyinat mā fī ṣuḥuf al-ūlā?” — “Has there not come to them clear evidence of what was in the earlier records?” | The verse challenges deniers who demand new miracles despite already having al-ṣuḥuf al-ʾūlā (earliest scriptures). | Clearly textual — refers to previous written revelations.

Q 53:36–37 | “Am lam yunaḇḇaʾ bimā fī ṣuḥuf Mūsā wa-Ibrāhīm…” | Invokes the written teachings of Moses and Abraham. | Written scriptures—explicitly described as ṣuḥuf belonging to named prophets.

Q 74:52 | “Kullu mriʾin minhum yurīdu an yuʾtā ṣuḥufan munashsharah.” | Describes arrogant deniers who demand that scrolls be physically handed to each of them. | Literal writing—they want tangible scrolls opened/unrolled for themselves.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
Q 80:13–15 | “Fī ṣuḥufin mukarramah marfūʿah muṭahharah bi-aydī safarah…” | Portrays revelation as inscribed in honorable, purified pages handled by scribes. | Explicitly written pages, handled and transmitted through scribal mediation.

Q 87:18–19 | “Ṣuḥuf Ibrāhīm wa Mūsā.” | Cites the enduring written legacy of previous prophets. | Again, written revelation, archetypal “pages.”

Accordingly, Q 98:2 — “reciting purified ṣuḥuf” — implies engagement with actual written pages. This meaning is linguistically reinforced by every other revelatory use of ṣuḥuf across the Qurʾān. The Qurʾānic semantic field of ṣuḥuf thus confirms that writing was intrinsic to revelation from the outset.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
وَالطُّورِ وَكِتَابٍ مَسْطُورٍ فِي رَقٍّ مَنْشُورٍ

Wa-al-ṭūr(i) wa-kitābin masṭūr(in) fī raqqin manshūr(in)

“By the Mount, and by a Book inscribed, In parchment spread open.” (Q 52:2–3)

Here, revelation is explicitly tied to writing — a kitāb masṭūr, a book inscribed upon raqq, meaning parchment or fine writing skin. The adjective masṭūr (مَسْطُور) derives from the root س-ط-ر (s-ṭ-r), meaning “to write in lines or to arrange in order by writing.”

As recorded in Lane’s Arabic–English Lexicon (Vol. 4, p. 1319):

“سَطَرَ — He wrote, or drew lines, or arranged in writing; hence masṭūr signifies ‘written, lined, inscribed.’ The term applies to what is set forth in writing, arranged in lines upon a page.”

Similarly, raqq (رَقّ) denotes a thin surface prepared for writing — usually fine parchment made from animal skin (Lane Vol. 1, p. 1164).

This oath (Q 52:2–3) places the Book within a material and scribal context: revelation is already inscribed, existing in written form, not merely as a recited utterance. The Qurʾān therefore presents itself as a textual revelation, implying a Prophet familiar with the concept and medium of writing — a message both preserved and manifested through the act of inscription.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.section: 3.3. Q 80:13–16 — “In honored pages, in the hands of scribes”
chunks.text:
فِي صُحُفٍ مُّكَرَّمَةٍ مَّرْفُوعَةٍ مُّطَهَّرَةٍ بِأَيْدِي سَفَرَةٍ كِرَامٍ بَرَرَةٍ

Fī ṣuḥufin mukarramah, marfūʿatin muṭahharah, bi-aydī safarah kirāmin bararah.

“upon pages high-honoured, uplifted, purified, by the hands of scribes — noble, pious” (Q 80:13–16)

The revelation is portrayed as ṣuḥuf — “written pages” or “scrolls” — handled by safarah, meaning scribes. The term safarah derives from the triliteral root س-ف-ر (s-f-r), which in classical Arabic denotes “to uncover, to make manifest, to bring to light.”

As LANE’s Lexicon notes (Vol. 1, p. 1413):

“سَفَرَ — He uncovered, revealed, or made manifest a thing that was concealed; hence al-sifr (book) is so called because it discloses or makes manifest knowledge written therein.”

This linguistic background shows that sāfir —and its plural safarah — describes those who make revelation manifest, i.e., scribes who inscribe divine communication in written form. Hence the verse reinforces revelation as a written and textual phenomenon, not merely an oral recital. It depicts a process of transmission involving scribes of high moral standing, suggesting that the Qurʾān was being written down, copied, and preserved from its earliest phase of revelation, ready for dissemination among the believers.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
The vivid imagery described in Q 68:1 and Q 96:4 indirectly provides further evidence of a writing culture within the community that lacked exposure to any prior revelation.

نٓ وَٱلْقَلَمِ وَمَا يَسْطُرُونَ

Nūn. Wa-al-qalami wa-mā yasṭurūn.

“Nūn. By the pen and what they inscribe.” (68:1)

ٱلَّذِى عَلَّمَ بِٱلْقَلَمِ

Alladhī ʿallama bi-al-qalam.

“Who taught by the pen.” (96:4)

These verses suggest literacy within the recipients of the Qurʾān and that writing was intrinsic to revelation from the very beginning.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
This is the longest verse in the Qurʾān and it commands that contracts be written down. It exhorts believers to “let a scribe write,” “do not refuse to write” and “do not be weary of writing it, whether big or small” suggesting that there was a culture of reading and writing during the time of Muhammad. There were scribes who wrote and preservation through writing was common in serious matters.

This suggests that a civilization capable of documenting complex debt contracts would obviously document revelation.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.section: 3.6. The Qurʾān as “al-Kitāb”: A Written Revelation
chunks.text:
Beyond individual verses, the Qurʾān repeatedly refers to itself as al-Kitāb — “the Book.” This term alone signals a written and recorded reality, not a purely oral composition.

The root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b) means “to write, to inscribe, to record.” As LANE’s Lexicon explains (Vol. 7, p. 2620):

“كَتَبَ — He wrote, or inscribed characters or words; he caused to be recorded in writing.”

Thus, when the Qurʾān opens with ذَٰلِكَ الْكِتَابُ لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ (dhālika al-kitāb lā rayba fīh, Q 2:2) — “That is the Book in which there is no doubt” — it identifies itself explicitly as a written text. The demonstrative dhālika points to something present and recognizable, while kitāb denotes a documented record. The numerous occurrences of al-kitāb throughout the Qurʾān (e.g., Q 2:2; Q 3:3; Q 6:7; Q 17:58; Q 29:48) reinforce this self-understanding: revelation was inscribed, preserved, and transmitted in written form from the outset.

This stands in contrast to later extra-Qurʾānic traditions that depict the Qurʾān as a primarily oral corpus compiled only under the caliph ʿUthmān. The Qurʾān’s own language leaves no room for that assumption — it presents itself as a text already written, read, and engaged with by the Prophet and his community.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
Modern Qurʾānic philology has increasingly challenged the traditional chronology that confines the Qurʾān’s written codification to the caliphate of ʿUthmān. As ANGELIKA NEUWIRTH notes,

“Evidence of old Qurʾān codices (see PUIN 1996) as well as new philological (DE BLOIS 2002) and historical (AMMAN; DONNER 1998; DOSTAL 1991; KRONE 1992) studies have provided strong arguments in favor of the Qurʾān’s emergence from an Arabian environment and of an early date of the Qurʾān redaction, thus advocating for the fixation of the text in the shape transmitted to us.” – In the Blackwell Companion to the Qurʾān, ed. ANDREW RIPPIN (Chichester: Wiley-Blackwell, 2009), 141.

She situates the Qurʾān within the literary and scriptural culture of Late Antiquity, arguing that its textual form “emerged from and dialogued with the written cultures of Jewish and Christian Late Antiquity” (NEUWIRTH 2019, 3).

Codicological research by PUIN and others reinforces this reassessment of the Qurʾān’s early written transmission. As NEUWIRTH (2009) observes, GERD R. PUIN’s study of the Ṣanʿāʾ palimpsests revealed textual features characteristic of first-century AH writing:

“A few of these Qurʾānic manuscripts displayed signs of great antiquity, allowing them to be placed with a degree of certitude into the first century of the Hijra” (PUIN 1996, 110).

He concludes that “the textual history of the Qurʾān is more complex than traditionally assumed,” implying contemporaneous written activity during the Prophet’s lifetime (ibid., 112).

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
Palimpsest studies of Ṣanʿāʾ 1 have further shown that the parchment dates from the first half of the seventh century A.D. and that its text does not belong to the ʿUthmānic textual tradition. The lower writing represents “the only known manuscript of a non-ʿUthmānic text type,” identified through palaeographic and art-historical analysis. Radiocarbon testing assigns the parchment—and hence the lower codex—to a period before A.D. 671 with a probability of 99 percent (before 661 with 95.5 percent; before 646 with 75 percent) (SADEGHI and GOUDARZI 2012, 1–3). This places it significantly earlier than other Qurʾānic manuscripts dated so far.

The Birmingham manuscript (University of Birmingham, Mingana 1572a) has likewise been radiocarbon-dated to 568–645 CE CE (95.4% probability), overlapping with the Prophet’s lifetime. While the dating applies to the writing material rather than the ink, the manuscript nonetheless constitutes one of the earliest extant witnesses to the Qurʾānic text (FEDELI 2018).

Such evidence points to an active scribal milieu during or immediately after the Prophet’s life rather than an exclusively oral preservation awaiting later codification. Historically and empirically, the claim of early written transmission can now be tested and verified: the Qurʾān’s text has remained consistent from the earliest surviving manuscripts of the seventh century CE to modern printed editions.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text: Collectively, these studies lend empirical weight to a linguistic reading of the Qurʾān that recognizes writing as intrinsic to revelation. The convergence of internal linguistic evidence and external manuscript data supports the thesis advanced here: that the Qurʾān was being written from its inception, and that later notions of prophetic illiteracy or delayed compilation arose from theological rather than linguistic premises.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
This study does not seek to diminish the long-standing reverence Muslims hold for the Qurʾān and its Messenger; rather, it seeks to affirm and elevate that reverence by returning to the Qurʾān’s own linguistic evidence. By allowing the text to speak in its own terms, the study clarifies how certain theological interpretations—such as prophetic illiteracy and delayed codification—evolved historically and came to replace the Qurʾān’s own self-description over time.

For more than a millennium, Muslim exegetes, philologists, and historians have sought to explain the miraculous nature of the Qurʾān. In doing so, they developed interpretive frameworks that emphasized divine intervention over human agency—among them the notion that the Prophet was “illiterate” and that the Qurʾān’s preservation occurred only through a later official codification. These explanations were not born out of malice but from a deep desire to defend revelation against skepticism and to highlight its divine origin.

However, linguistic and textual analysis of the Qurʾān itself reveals a more nuanced picture: one that strengthens, rather than weakens, the miracle of revelation. If the Qurʾān shows that the Prophet engaged directly with writing, this does not diminish the divine message—it instead attests to a revelation perfectly suited to its Messenger and his context. Similarly, evidence that the Qurʾān was written during the Prophet’s lifetime affirms the very precision and care with which divine words were recorded and transmitted.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
Re-examining inherited assumptions, therefore, is not an act of defiance but an act of faithfulness—to the Qurʾān’s own language and testimony, which affirms that the gathering, recitation and clarification of the message originate from the divine (Q 75:16-19).

“Upon Us is its gathering and its recitation [...] Then upon Us is its clarification.” (75:16-19)

The intention here is not to replace one dogma with another, but to invite readers to engage the text as it speaks, without intermediaries. Such inquiry belongs to a long and respected tradition within Islam, where scholars—from al-Zamakhsharī to Muʿtazilite grammarians—pursued meaning through language, reason, and evidence.

A comparable pan-textual linguistic approach has been applied in a separate study of Qurʾān Q 65:4, demonstrating that the verse—often cited in debates on child marriage—when read contextually, upholds marriage as a contractual union between mature, accountable partners rather than as a sanction of prepubescent marriage (SAMIN and MALIK 2025). Both studies exemplify how a Qurʾān-centric linguistic method can clarify the text’s ethical and theological coherence without reliance on later exegetical constructions grounded in assumed conclusions, revealing that the Qurʾān’s internal linguistic architecture is ethically and intellectually self-consistent once freed from inherited interpretation.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
Ultimately, acknowledging that some post-Qurʾānic interpretations were shaped by historical apologetics does not diminish but rather elevates the sanctity of revelation. It reminds us that human interpretation, however sincere, remains fallible when measured against the Qurʾān’s own morphological and syntactic precision. As the Qurʾān declares:

“Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it; [it is] a revelation from a [Lord who is] Wise and Praiseworthy.” (Q 41:42)

Conclusion — Qurʾānic Language vs. Later Tradition

A pan-textual linguistic reading of the Qurʾān stands in tension with later exegetical and ḥadīth-based portrayals of an “illiterate Prophet.” Within the Qurʾān, the word ʾummī means “unscriptured,” not illiterate (Q 2:78). Muḥammad was ummī only in the sense of being raised among a people “who did not know the Book” (Q 62:2).

Once revelation began, he became the reader, teacher, and transmitter of a written Book. Verses such as (Q 25:5; 98:2; 52:2–3; 80:13–15; 29:48; 2:282; 68:1; 96:4) depict a Prophet operating within a culture of writing and reading.

The Qurʾān presents itself as a written text (al-kitāb) from the very beginning which is in tension with extra-Qurʾānic historical claims that it was compiled only later during the reign of ʿUthmān. This internal Qurʾānic evidence is consistent with and not contradicted by the Ṣanʿāʾ 1 and Birmingham Manuscript radiocarbon dating record discussed earlier.

chunks.title: Reassessing Prophetic Literacy and the Written Transmission of Revelation: A Linguistic and Textual Analysis of the Qurʾān
chunks.text:
The Qurʾān’s own morphology, syntax, and semantics therefore indicate that Muḥammad could read and write, and that his “unlettered” status referred not to literacy but to the absence of prior exposure to any scripture. Its internal evidence—from the precision of its verbs (iktatabahā), to its repeated self-reference as kitāb, to its vivid imagery of ṣuḥuf (pages), safarah (scribes) writing with their hands and qalam (pen)—reveals a revelation conceived, transmitted, and preserved through writing.

The Qurʾān self-describes revelation through terms that intrinsically presuppose writing—kitāb, ṣuḥuf, raqq, masṭūr, safarah, qalam. In its own language, the Qurʾān affirms a Prophet who could read and write—not an “unlettered” man reciting words he could not comprehend, but a dutiful Messenger entrusted with reading, writing, teaching, and preserving “the Book in which there is no doubt.”
